Importantly, this configuration would 2 require finding a location for bulk LH storage that is directly adjacent to the tarmac such that the 2 aircraft and storage tanks are within a reasonable distance from each other while also meeting separation distance requirements yet to determined. This could be very difficult for airports to accommodate depending on space constraints. Also, in this scenario an aircraft would not refuel at the passenger loading terminal and therefore could not take advantage of unloading and loading passengers or cargo at the same time as refueling. Conventional aircraft are typically refueled at the terminal gate such that passenger or cargo loading and unloading can occur at the same time and reduce total grounded time (Bracci et al. 2026; SKYbrary n.d.). For the mobile refueling configuration, mobile refueling trucks would pick up LH from the bulk 2 storage and dispense it into an aircraft either at the terminal gate or at designated refueling locations. This configuration is advantageous over fixed refueling next to bulk storage in that the bulk storage does not need to be directly next to the tarmac, opening up more locations for placing bulk storage at or nearby the airport. It is not yet clear whether mobile refuelers will be allowed to dispense at the terminal gate because safety zones for liquid hydrogen dispensing are not established. In addition, even if safety zones are established that do allow for dispensing at the terminal gate, this does not necessarily mean that dispensing can occur while passengers are on board the aircraft. Current regulations state that an aircraft may be fueled with kerosene-based fuels (e.g., Jet A) but not fuels containing gasoline (e.g., Jet B) with passengers on board (Bracci et al. 2026; SKYbrary n.d.). This is due to the higher flammability of gasoline mixtures compared to kerosene. Considering hydrogen is even more flammable than gasoline-containing jet fuel, LH refueling 2 would likely not be allowed while passengers are on board under current regulations. However, hydrogen’s thermal, chemical, and physical characteristics are much different than Jet A and Jet B, and further research must be carried out such that LH -specific regulations on this topic can 2 be implemented. In a hydrant and dispenser truck configuration, the bulk cryogenic storage tanks would be connected to cryogenic distribution pipelines that end at designated refueling points with a 77 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. hydrant system. A dispenser truck with cryogenic pumps would connect the hydrant to the onboard aircraft storage tank using insulated transfer lines (Hoelzen et al. 2022; Airport Compatibility of Alternative Aviation Fuels Task Force, International Industry Working Group 2025). This is a longer-term solution than refueling directly adjacent to the bulk storage or using mobile refuelers because the distribution pipeline technology is not yet commercial and because this configuration is only economically viable at large demand levels.
